A professional website in Cyprus real estate is not about design trends. It is about creating digital authority that supports premium positioning.

Launching a real estate agency in Cyprus — especially in the premium segment — requires more than an attractive website. It requires structured digital architecture, multilingual positioning, and long-term search visibility.

A property developer website is not a business card or a "pretty picture on the internet." It is a sales tool through which buyers find your projects, study floor plans, compare options and submit inquiries. How well it is built directly determines how many inquiries you get from search and how many of them turn into real deals.

The price range for real estate website development is huge — from a few thousand euros to tens of thousands. The reason is not that someone is "overcharging," but that the phrase "developer website" covers projects of fundamentally different complexity. Several factors shape the final cost.

Quick answer: monitoring is the audit repeated on a schedule. Run the same fixed prompt set monthly, in a clean session, across the same platforms, and track four numbers: how many answers named you, how many contained an error, which sources were cited, and how many visits arrived from assistant referrals. Everything else is detail. The hard part isn't collecting the data — it's telling a real change from the natural variation between runs, which is why the set and the conditions have to stay identical.

Most definitions of GEO are one paragraph long and borrowed from each other. This article starts from primary sources: the paper that coined the term, two large studies of where AI engines take their sources, the documentation Google, OpenAI and Microsoft publish for site owners, my own analysis of 141 AI answers to buying questions, and a live check on 23 October 2026 of how Google and Perplexity answer the question «what is generative engine optimization» itself. That last check turned out to be the best example of GEO in this article.

Accuracy is part of the job. An answer can name you with an old price, a service you dropped or a feature that belongs to a competitor. I describe those cases in where AI gets outdated information about your company.

A second naming problem: GEO, AEO (answer engine optimization), LLMO (large language model optimization) and AIO (AI optimization) are used interchangeably by many writers, and both Google's AI Overview and Perplexity repeat that in their answers. They overlap but they are not identical: AEO is narrower and is about your wording becoming the answer to one specific question. The differences, with examples, are in GEO vs SEO vs AEO.
Answer engine optimization on its own — how one answer is chosen and how to become its source — is covered in what is AEO.

For service questions, Perplexity and AI Mode built their answers largely from the providers' own websites, while ChatGPT leaned on its own search and on map listings. Changes take about a day to reach ChatGPT search. Generative engines merge sources. If your website says you were founded in 2015, LinkedIn says 2017 and an old directory lists a previous address, the answer may contain any combination. The work here is unglamorous: list the twenty facts that define your business — name, services, prices or price ranges, locations, languages, founders, years, key clients you can name — and make them identical on your site, Google Business Profile, LinkedIn, directories and any review platforms. The most common sources of wrong answers, and how to fix them, are in how to correct wrong information in ChatGPT.

Ask each one in ChatGPT, Perplexity, Google AI Mode and Gemini once a month, in a clean session. Record three things: whether you are named, whether you are cited with a link, and whether the description is correct. Strona psychologa praktykującego we Włoszech. Praktyka prywatna z górnej półki, gdzie decyduje osoba wybierająca, komu powierzyć pieniądze, czas i sprawy dość osobiste.

W praktyce część tych stron zostanie przeskanowana i odrzucona — status „przeskanowana, obecnie niezindeksowana" (Crawled – currently not indexed) — a to nie ma już nic wspólnego z mapą witryny. Decyduje o tym, czy strona zasługuje na miejsce: czy cokolwiek do niej linkuje, czy mówi coś, czego w indeksie jeszcze nie ma, czy witryna ma na tyle mocną pozycję, żeby wybaczono jej cienkie podstrony.
Całkowity koszt przebiegu: około półtora dolara. Metoda jest odtwarzalna dla dowolnej domeny i opisana krok po kroku w osobnym tekście o tym, jak sprawdzić, co AI mówi o Twojej firmie.
Ten tekst nie jest o tym, że „każda firma potrzebuje strony" — taki poradnik napisałem osobno dla kancelarii prawnych. Jest o konkretnych liczbach z Google Ads i o tym, kto dziś zbiera te zapytania.

Jest w tym dobra wiadomość dla małego biura. Odpowiedź AI cytuje stronę, która odpowiada najkonkretniej, niekoniecznie największą. Wasza wiedza operacyjna — ile realnie czeka się teraz na kartę pobytu w waszym urzędzie wojewódzkim, czego naprawdę brakuje w odrzucanych wnioskach — jest dokładnie tym rodzajem treści, którego nie ma na stronie urzędu. Co trzeba zrobić technicznie, żeby te treści w ogóle trafiły do odpowiedzi, opisuję w przygotowaniu strony do wyszukiwania AI.

Strona wielojęzyczna zrobiona dobrze to nie przetłumaczony polski tekst. To osobny adres dla każdego języka, własne słowa kluczowe w tym języku (bo Ukrainiec szuka inaczej niż Polak), poprawne znaczniki hreflang, żeby Google wiedział, komu pokazać którą wersję, i formularz w języku, w którym klient jest gotów napisać. Tworzenie stron wielojęzycznych opisuję osobno, bo to najczęstsza przyczyna utraconych zapytań w tej branży.

Zasada była ta sama, co opisałem wyżej: każda procedura i każdy kraj na własnym adresie, kwoty i terminy podane liczbami zamiast „zapytaj o ofertę", każdy język pisany od zera pod własne zapytania, a nie tłumaczony, wszystkie dane z podaniem źródła. Pełny opis z liczbami jest w studium przypadku tego projektu.

Jeśli odpowiedź jest „nigdzie", to nie problem reklamy, tylko brak stron, które odpowiadają na te zapytania. Napiszcie do mnie — powiem, które procedury z waszej oferty mają realny popyt w wyszukiwarce, a które nie warte są osobnej strony.

Profil w Google i pozycjonowanie lokalne są konieczne i działają na zapytania z nazwą miasta. Ale nie zajmie miejsca na „legalizację zatrudnienia cudzoziemców", bo to nie zapytanie lokalne, i nie zostanie zacytowany w odpowiedzi AI jako źródło procedury. Do tego potrzebne są strony z treścią.
Dlatego treść o procedurach trzyma się w systemie zarządzania, w którym wasz zespół sam zmienia liczby i terminy, bez programisty. To warunek, nie dodatek — patrz utrzymanie strony internetowej.

llms.txt to proponowany plik Markdown w katalogu głównym strony, który wymienia jej najważniejsze podstrony dla modeli językowych. Często sprzedaje się go jako «robots.txt dla AI», a nim nie jest: niczego nie może dopuścić ani zablokować. Google pisze, że jego systemy wyszukiwania go nie używają, a żadne opublikowane badanie nie wykazało, że zwiększa liczbę cytowań w odpowiedziach AI. Może się przydać stronom z dokumentacją, której użytkownicy wklejają ją do asystentów programistycznych. Dla widoczności w ChatGPT, Claude czy Perplexity liczą się robots.txt i czytelny HTML, a llms.txt — nie. Szczegóły z przykładowym plikiem są w artykule czy strona potrzebuje pliku llms.txt.

llms.txt — предлагаемый файл в формате Markdown в корне сайта, который перечисляет его главные страницы для языковых моделей. Его часто продают как «robots.txt для ИИ», но это не так: он ничего не может разрешить или запретить. Google пишет, что его поисковые системы файл не используют, и ни одно опубликованное исследование не показало, что он увеличивает число цитирований в ответах ИИ. Он может пригодиться сайтам с документацией, которую пользователи вставляют в ассистенты для программирования. Для видимости в ChatGPT, Claude или Perplexity важны robots.txt и читаемый HTML, а llms.txt — нет. Подробности с примером файла — в статье нужен ли сайту файл llms.txt.

Ту же работу называют «продвижением в ChatGPT» или «оптимизацией под поиск ChatGPT». Это часть более широкого LLM SEO, применённая к одному ассистенту.

Это руководство идёт по работам в том порядке, в котором я делал бы их сам: с данными под каждым решением и с правилами, из-за которых профили компаний действительно блокируют. И одно разграничение, которое экономит месяцы: продвижение сайта — это не создание сайта. Если на сайте нечего продвигать, порядок другой: сначала структура и страницы, потом видимость. Как выглядит сайт, собранный сразу под поиск, я описываю на странице сайт для малого бизнеса; дальше я исхожу из того, что сайт у вас уже есть.

Это стоит знать до того, как покупать что-либо под названием «оптимизация под ИИ». Настоящая работа над видимостью в ИИ есть: проверять, что ассистенты говорят о вашей компании, править неверные данные в источнике и измерять это во времени. Я разбираю её ниже и подробно — в статье о том, что такое GEO. Но это не новый набор технических требований, и кто продаёт его как технический продукт, продаёт страницу настроек, которой, по словам Google, не существует.

Дальше сделайте название, адрес и телефон одинаковыми на сайте, в профиле и в каждом каталоге. Расхождения здесь — одна из немногих чисто механических вещей, которые до сих пор тормозят локальную выдачу. Профиль — только половина локальной картины: как блок карт и сайт работают вместе, я разбираю на странице про локальное SEO-продвижение.

Внешняя помощь отрабатывает деньги в четырёх местах: аудит, который прямо говорит, может ли поиск работать для вашего бизнеса; технические правки, для которых нужен человек, умеющий нормально править сайт; тексты в конкурентных услугах и на неродном для вас языке; и измерение, которое связывает поиск с реальными обращениями, а не с позициями. Для бизнеса такого размера это обычно один человек, а не агентство: как это выглядит на практике, описано на странице частный SEO-специалист.

Эти три дела ничего не стоят и занимают вечер. Зато они показывают, где вы находитесь, — а это больше, чем даёт большинство аудитов. Если хочется, чтобы на остальное посмотрел кто-то со стороны, напишите мне: пришлите сайт, основную услугу и территорию, которую вы охватываете, и я скажу, что сделал бы первым — включая, если это окажется честным ответом, что поиск вам не подходит как канал.

Совсем другое дело — работа над тем, чтобы сайт находили. Это не обслуживание, а работа с секундомером, и она устроена иначе: первые сдвиги примерно через полтора месяца, устойчивый рост через три-шесть месяцев. Сколько это стоит и из чего состоит, я разобрал отдельно в статье про стоимость продвижения сайта, чтобы не повторять это здесь.

SEO-аудит — 250 €, разово. Его разумнее делать до переделки, а не после: он показывает, какие страницы уже имеют ценность, которую стоит сохранить. Постоянная работа по поиску — от 800 € в месяц, и это другая услуга с другими сроками: первые сдвиги примерно через полтора месяца, устойчивый рост через три-шесть месяцев. Если хотите число от меня, напишите мне: услуги, города, в которых вы работаете, и ссылка на то, что у вас есть сейчас — сайт, профиль в соцсети, карточка на картах. Я скажу, что бы я сделал, сколько это будет стоить и что я бы не делал, включая те случаи, когда честный ответ — что вам нужна карточка на картах и телефон, а не сайт.

Присутствие в ответах ИИ. Показывается ли ответ ИИ по запросам, на которые целится сайт, и есть ли сайт хоть где-то в том пуле, из которого эти ответы собираются — на это и отвечает аудит видимости в ИИ-поиске. В примере: ответ ИИ показался по 304 семействам запросов из 321, а сайт не попал в первую десятку ни по одному из них.

Полный аудит занимает от двух до пяти рабочих дней, а его цена и состав описаны на странице услуги. В эту сумму должны входить измерение с источниками, упорядоченный план, ожидаемый результат по каждому действию и разговор после прочтения. В неё не должно входить внедрение — это другая работа с другой ценой, а их склейка превращает аудит в продающий документ для той работы, которую он же и рекомендует.

Someone looking for a cleaning company arrives with two questions in mind. What will this cost, and can I trust these people in my home. Almost every site in the field answers the first with "contact us" and the second not at all. The price question is the more surprising omission, because cleaning is genuinely calculable. Area, number of rooms, frequency, whether it's routine or post-renovation — a handful of inputs produces a defensible estimate. A calculator that returns a number on the spot converts a large share of visitors who would never have filled in an enquiry form just to ask what it costs, and it filters out those whose expectations were never going to match. I've built parameter-based calculators of exactly this kind, where a few selections produce a price immediately.

Most studio websites are structured as if the visitor wants to read about the studio. They don't. They want to know whether a class they're interested in runs at a time they can actually attend, near enough to reach, with a way to try it once before committing to anything. Everything else on the site is secondary to that sequence. This is what website development looks like when the structure comes first.

Which makes the timetable the most important object on the page, and it's the one most often handled worst — published as an image or a downloadable file, unreadable on a phone, impossible to filter by class type or instructor, and out of date within a week. A schedule that's wrong once costs more than the effort of maintaining it properly, because a person who turned up for a class that doesn't exist rarely gives a second chance. Whether that comes from a page builder or custom-built code is a decision worth making deliberately, not by default.

The second structural gap is the missing first step. Studios sell memberships, and membership is a commitment people don't make from a website they've just found. Between interest and commitment there needs to be something low-stakes — a trial class, a single visit, a short pack — with its own clear path that doesn't route through a monthly plan. That first visit is the conversion the site should be built around; retention is what the studio does afterwards, and it's a different job.

Then instructors. In group fitness people follow a person more than a place — the class they book is often the one taught by someone specific. Studios whose teachers have no presence on the site are missing the part of the decision that actually drives both the first booking and the return.

Hotels are among the few businesses where the value of their own website can be calculated exactly. Every reservation made through a booking platform carries a commission — a double-digit percentage of the stay — and along with it goes the guest relationship: their contact details, their preferences, the ability to reach them again. A booking taken on your own site carries neither cost. The difference is not marketing theory; it's a line in the accounts. This is what website development looks like when the structure comes first.

Which is what makes the common situation strange. Most hotel websites don't take bookings at all. A guest arrives, likes what they see, and then goes back to a platform to reserve — because that's where the button was. The site did the work of persuading and handed the transaction to someone who charges for it.

Fixing that starts with the booking path itself, integrated with whatever system you already use so a reservation can be completed without leaving your site. But a booking engine alone doesn't change behaviour, because guests genuinely believe platforms are cheaper or safer. Whatever advantage you can offer for booking direct has to be stated where the decision is being made — plainly, not buried in a policies page.

Language is the other half, and it's more technical than it looks. Guests arrive from many countries and search in their own languages, so versions aren't optional for most properties. But translation is the easy part: without correct routing and markup, the versions compete with each other and the site performs worse than a single-language one would. I've built multilingual sites whose visitors come from more than twenty countries, and what makes that work is the structure underneath rather than the words on top.

And finally the images. Hotels are chosen visually, so photography is the product — and photography is also what makes hotel sites slow, particularly on the phones where most browsing happens. That's solvable without compromising quality: on a client project with a large gallery, the right approach took mobile performance from around 50 to 92 while the images stayed exactly as they were. I've built exactly that kind of multilingual, image-heavy site for a real estate client whose buyers come from more than twenty countries.

Language schools have an unusual traffic pattern. For most of the year the site ticks along; then enrolment season arrives and a large share of the year's decisions get made in a matter of weeks. That concentration changes what matters. A structure that's merely adequate in March costs real groups in September, because everyone who hesitates during the window doesn't come back later — they come back next term, if at all. This is what website development looks like when the structure comes first.

What survives that window is a site where a person can complete the decision themselves. That means course information readable on the page rather than in a downloadable timetable, prices visible, formats compared side by side, and — critically — a way to sign up and pay without a phone call. Enrolment completed at the moment of decision is a different conversion rate from enrolment that requires a callback tomorrow. I've implemented Stripe payments on a client's educational product for exactly this reason: taking course fees directly on the site rather than deferring the transaction.

Industrial buying differs from almost every other kind in one respect: the person searching usually knows precisely what they're looking for before they start. A material in a grade. A component within a tolerance. A process for a given volume. A supplier holding a particular certification. They aren't browsing for inspiration, and they aren't going to be persuaded by a description of your company's values. This is what website development looks like when the structure comes first.

Which is why the standard manufacturing website underperforms. It opens with when the company was founded, its commitment to quality and its modern machinery — while the visitor is trying to establish whether you can produce a specific part in a specific alloy at a specific volume. If the answer isn't on the page in the form they're looking for, they leave, and they leave without contacting you, because there was nothing to suggest an enquiry would be worth their time.

Finally, language. Manufacturers export as a matter of routine, and technical searches happen in the buyer's own language. A site in a single language is absent from most of the markets the company already sells into — and the fix is structural rather than linguistic: versions with correct routing and markup work independently, while incorrectly configured ones compete with each other and can leave a site worse off than before. Getting that multilingual structure right is what makes the difference, the same way a filterable product catalogue makes a large range findable.

Choosing a photographer is unlike choosing most services. There's no specification to compare and little to research — the decision is made by looking, quickly, and asking whether this person's work looks like what I want my own photographs to look like. Everything the site does either supports that judgement or gets in its way. Whether that comes from a page builder or custom-built code is a decision worth making deliberately, not by default.

Two questions then arrive with nearly every enquiry: what it costs, and whether you're free on a particular date. Both can be handled on the page. Packages with prices — or at least a starting figure — filter enquiries down to people whose expectations match. And for date-driven work, an enquiry form that captures the date up front means your first reply is an answer rather than a question, which in a field where couples contact five photographers at once is a meaningful advantage.

Finally, delivery. Most photographers hand over finished work through expiring transfer links, and then field requests to re-upload months later. Private galleries on your own site make delivery part of the experience rather than an afterthought — and it's the last impression a client takes away, which they'll repeat to whoever asks them for a recommendation. This is what website development looks like when the structure comes first.

Almost every visit to a restaurant website is driven by one of three questions: what do they serve, are they open, and can I get a table. Answering those three on a phone within a few seconds is most of what the site is for. Everything else — the story, the interiors, the chef's biography — matters only to visitors who got past those first questions satisfied.

Which makes the standard habit of publishing the menu as a PDF the most expensive decision in the field. It fails on all three counts at once. On a phone it requires pinching and zooming to read, which is enough to lose people. It's invisible to search engines, so the restaurant competes only for its own name rather than for the food it actually serves. And because updating it means regenerating a file, it drifts out of date until the version people are reading isn't the one being cooked.

Publishing the menu as ordinary pages fixes all of it. Dishes become text your kitchen can change the same day, readable without effort, and — with the right structured data — legible to search engines and AI assistants, which increasingly answer questions like "where can I eat something specific nearby" with a short list rather than a page of links. People search for dishes and cuisines far more than for restaurant names, and a menu locked in a file participates in none of that. Whether that comes from a page builder or custom-built code is a decision worth making deliberately, not by default.

Then there's the part most restaurant sites leave almost invisible: private events. Group bookings and closed events are frequently the most profitable evenings of a month, and on the majority of sites they amount to a sentence in the contact page. Giving them a real page — capacities, formats, what's possible, how far ahead to ask — makes them plannable, which is the only way anyone books them. This is what website development looks like when the structure comes first.

Logistics companies have an unusual problem: the website has two entirely separate audiences, and both are scarce. Clients with cargo to move, and drivers to move it. Most sites in this field are built for the first and treat the second as an afterthought in the footer — which, in an industry where finding drivers is as hard as finding contracts, wastes half of what the site could do. This is what website development looks like when the structure comes first.

On the client side, the recurring failure is the enquiry itself. Transport pricing depends on a specific set of facts: route, cargo type, weight, dimensions, dates, any special handling. A generic contact form gathers none of them, so every enquiry begins with an exchange of emails establishing what a properly structured form would have asked once. For some services the same inputs can produce an indicative figure immediately — I've built parameter-based calculators where a few selections return a price on the spot, and the principle transfers directly.

Then there's what happens after the contract. Once cargo is moving, clients want to know where it is, and without any way to check, that question arrives by phone. A status lookup solves it cheaply — I've implemented order status checking by phone number for a client, and it removed a large share of routine calls from their office.

And back to drivers. They search for work like everyone else, and they compare employers on concrete things: routes, equipment, how pay is structured, how often they're home. A recruitment section written for them, in the languages they actually speak, competes for attention in a market where every operator is short-handed. Multilingual structure matters here for a reason it doesn't elsewhere — the language your clients read and the language your drivers read may have nothing to do with each other.

From €2,000. The main variables are how complex the quote request needs to be, whether you want shipment status lookup, how many transport types need their own pages, and how many languages. Describe your company and I'll prepare a quote.

Travel agencies operate under a condition that most businesses don't: their customers can, in principle, do the job themselves. Flights and accommodation are a browser tab away, and everyone knows it. So every visitor arrives with an unspoken question — what does going through you actually add — and the site either answers it or loses to the alternative by default. This is what website development looks like when the structure comes first.

Then there's where visitors come from. People search for places long before they search for agencies: what a trip somewhere involves, when to go, what it costs, whether it suits a family. An agency that publishes real knowledge about the destinations it works with appears in those searches — at the moment when someone is deciding where to go rather than who to book with. Publishing that knowledge feels like giving something away, and it's the most reliable way this business gets found. It's also increasingly what AI assistants draw on when someone asks for advice on a destination. A multilingual real estate platform I built works the same way — the content earns visitors, not ads.

Finally, the structure of the offers themselves. Tours presented as static blocks or downloadable files can't be compared, and a visitor who can't compare on your site will do it somewhere they can. Filterable offers with each significant one on its own page solve both problems at once — the visitor compares where you want them to, and the pages behind the filters are what search engines can actually index. I've built filterable catalogues where exactly that structure is what brings the traffic. The same applies to language versions for agencies serving international clients.

Veterinary websites are visited under conditions that don't apply to most businesses. A significant share of visits happen when someone is frightened about an animal, often late in the evening, on a phone, with no patience for navigation. That single fact should shape the entire structure: whether you're open right now, the phone number and how to reach you belong in the first thing a visitor sees, not behind a menu. The same goes for booking the visit — it should be one tap away, not a phone call during business hours.

The rest of the site serves a calmer visitor, and there the structure differs from human healthcare in a specific way. Owners don't search by treatment first — they search by animal. A person with a rabbit or a parrot looks for a clinic that treats rabbits or parrots, because plenty don't, and a clinic that hasn't said so simply isn't in that search. Species and specialisation pages catch searches that a general services page cannot. Getting found for those searches is ongoing SEO work, not a one-time setup.

Price is unavoidable here in a way many clinics wish it weren't. Veterinary care is paid for directly, often unexpectedly, and owners search for specific procedures alongside their cost. A clinic that gives a range for common procedures does two things at once: it appears in those searches, and it stops fielding calls that were only ever about price.

One part deserves particular care rather than optimisation. Every clinic offers services around the end of an animal's life, and those pages need a different register entirely — quiet, factual, without marketing language. Handling that well says something about a practice that no amount of copy about compassion can. This is what website development looks like when the structure comes first.

The hesitation is almost always the same, and it's justified: the fear of losing rankings. That fear is well founded, because a badly executed migration does exactly that — and the damage is neither gradual nor self-correcting. A client of mine had a redesign pushed straight to production without checks: addresses changed with no redirects, language versions ended up swapped, structured data disappeared. Traffic started falling within two days and hadn't recovered a month later. Diagnosis and repair took two weeks, and the recovery took roughly another month after that.

What makes the difference isn't the platform chosen. It's whether the migration treats the old site's search equity as an asset to be transferred rather than a side effect that will hopefully survive. Concretely: a baseline recorded before anything moves, an address structure either preserved or mapped completely, metadata and structured data carried over deliberately, language versions rebuilt with correct routing, and the whole thing assembled on a staging environment before anyone sees it.

Done that way, a migration is unremarkable — which is the point. I moved a Warsaw workshop from an ageing platform to a custom-built WordPress theme: the address structure stayed intact, the markup came across, the four language versions kept working, and mobile performance went from around 50 to 92. The visible result was a faster, better site. The invisible result was that nothing was lost in the process, which is what the work was actually for. The same discipline applies when a startup outgrows its first platform.

What decides the outcome is how search engines are told which version belongs to which audience. That's the hreflang and canonical setup, and it's easy to get subtly wrong — the versions end up read as duplicates of one another, the ranking signal splits, and each version performs worse than a single-language site would have. This is the most common failure mode, and it's invisible: nothing looks broken, the traffic simply never arrives. Getting found in AI-generated answers depends on the same clean structure — I've seen a client get found through ChatGPT for exactly that reason.

Сомнение почти всегда одно и то же, и оно обоснованно: страх потерять позиции. У этого страха есть основания, потому что плохо проведённая миграция делает ровно это — и ущерб не постепенный и не самоисправляющийся. У моего клиента редизайн выкатили прямо на продакшен без проверки: адреса сменились без переадресации, языковые версии поменялись местами, структурированные данные исчезли. Трафик начал падать через два дня и через месяц не вернулся. Диагностика и починка заняли две недели, восстановление — ещё около месяца после них.

Площадь, количество помещений, периодичность, рутинная это уборка или после ремонта — нескольких параметров хватает для обоснованной оценки. Калькулятор, возвращающий цифру на месте, конвертирует заметную долю посетителей, которые никогда не заполнили бы форму только ради вопроса о стоимости, и отсеивает тех, чьи ожидания всё равно не совпали бы. Отели — из тех немногих бизнесов, где ценность собственного сайта считается точно. Каждая бронь через площадку несёт комиссию — двузначный процент от стоимости проживания, — а вместе с ней уходят отношения с гостем: его контакты, предпочтения, возможность обратиться к нему снова. Бронь, принятая на собственном сайте, не несёт ни одной из этих издержек. Разница не маркетинговая теория, а строка в отчёте. Так выглядит разработка сайта, когда структура стоит на первом месте.

Из-за этого обычная ситуация выглядит странно. Большинство сайтов отелей вообще не принимает брони. Гость заходит, ему нравится то, что он видит, и он возвращается бронировать на площадку — потому что кнопка была там. Сайт сделал работу по убеждению и отдал транзакцию тому, кто за неё берёт.

Починка начинается с самого пути бронирования, интегрированного с системой, которой вы уже пользуетесь, чтобы бронь можно было завершить, не уходя с сайта. Но один движок бронирования не меняет поведения, потому что гости искренне считают, что на площадках дешевле или безопаснее. Любое преимущество, которое вы можете дать за прямую бронь, должно быть сказано там, где принимается решение, — прямо, а не спрятано в правилах.

Язык — вторая половина, и она техничнее, чем выглядит. Гости приезжают из многих стран и ищут на своих языках, поэтому версии для большинства объектов не опция. Но перевод — лёгкая часть: без корректной маршрутизации и разметки версии конкурируют между собой, и сайт работает хуже, чем работал бы одноязычный. Я строил мультиязычные сайты, посетители которых приходят более чем из двадцати стран, и работает это благодаря структуре под текстом, а не словам на нём.

Именно это первое посещение — конверсия, вокруг которой стоит строить сайт; удержание студия делает позже и другими средствами.
